name: HackRF One
firmware_note: Stock firmware turns the board into a dumb USB radio front end; all signal processing happens on the host PC in GNU Radio, SDR++, SDRangel, etc.
price_note: Great Scott Gadgets still lists HackRF One, but the major US resellers have run dry: Hacker Warehouse shows it out of stock and states it 'is no longer being manufactured as it is replaced with the HackRF Pro', and Adafruit lists it at $339.95 'no longer stocked'. If you are buying new today, HackRF Pro ($400) is the unit actually in production. Sub-$150 'HackRF One' units on AliExpress/Amazon are clones - functional but often with a poor or absent TCXO, no RF shielding, and no revenue to the original developers.
skill_note: It is a bare RF front end - you supply the DSP knowledge, the antenna for the band, and the understanding of why your signal looks wrong.
build_note: Ships assembled in a plastic case. Antenna is NOT included; you need one per band you care about.
summary: A half-duplex, 8-bit software-defined radio covering 1 MHz to 6 GHz that both receives and transmits, tethered to a computer over USB 2.0. It is the reference open-source wideband SDR and the one nearly every RF security tutorial is written against. Great Scott Gadgets publishes the full schematics and firmware.
honest_take: Two specs people gloss over will bite you: it is 8-bit and it is half-duplex. Eight bits of ADC gives roughly 48 dB of dynamic range, so a strong nearby signal will bury everything else in the same capture - an RTL-SDR is 8-bit too, but a $150 Airspy or a 12-bit PlutoSDR will genuinely hear things a HackRF cannot. Half-duplex means it physically cannot listen while transmitting, which rules out the whole class of attacks that need to see a response mid-transmission. It is also a transmitter, and casually transmitting is how people get in real legal trouble.
best_for: Learning wideband SDR with the best-documented open hardware
RF replay and signal analysis across a very wide range
Feeding GNU Radio for research and CTF work
Serving as the radio half of a PortaPack handheld
not_for: Anyone who has not yet used an RTL-SDR - start there
Weak-signal work needing dynamic range (8-bit ADC)
Full-duplex protocols or anything needing simultaneous TX and RX
Above 6 GHz, or true DC/low-HF without an upconverter

hardware.mcu_primary_note: Main application processor; handles USB and baseband transfer. Official docs name the family as LPC43xx.

radios.note: 2.3-2.7 GHz direct-conversion transceiver, revisions r1-r8. Revision r9 uses the MAX2839 instead.
Wideband mixer/synthesizer that translates the whole 1 MHz-6 GHz range into the MAX2837's 2.3-2.7 GHz window.
8-bit ADC/DAC pair. This part is the reason HackRF is 8-bit.

hardware.battery_note: No battery. USB-powered and host-tethered unless paired with a PortaPack.
hardware.storage: W25Q80BV 8 Mbit SPI flash for firmware only
hardware.gpio: Internal pin headers for expansion (P9/P20/P22/P28 etc.), used by PortaPack and Opera Cake
notable_physical: SMA clock input and output for multi-unit synchronisation
Si5351C clock generator
Software-controlled 3.3V/50mA antenna port power for powering an LNA or bias tee

sdr_rx.note: 1 MHz to 6 GHz, 8-bit I/Q. Below ~10 MHz sensitivity falls off badly; an upconverter is the usual fix.

sdr_tx.note: Same 1 MHz-6 GHz range. Output power is low and varies a lot with frequency (roughly single-digit to low-teens dBm); GSG does not publish a flat figure.

sdr_bandwidth.note: Up to 20 Msps giving ~20 MHz of instantaneous bandwidth; baseband filter is software-configurable.

sdr_full_duplex.note: Half-duplex only. A single mixer and a single ADC/DAC path are shared between TX and RX - this is a hardware limit, not a firmware one.

subghz_rx.note: Covered as part of the general 1 MHz-6 GHz range, not via a dedicated sub-GHz transceiver.

subghz_tx.note: Same. No protocol decoding on-device - the host software does all of it.

subghz_replay.note: Trivially, by recording and replaying raw I/Q with hackrf_transfer. No rolling-code handling of any kind.

subghz_rolling_code.note: Nothing in hardware or stock firmware addresses rolling codes; replaying a captured rolling code does not work by design.

subghz_external_antenna.note: SMA female; you need a different antenna for each band of interest.

ble_sniff.note: 20 MHz of bandwidth cannot span BLE's 80 MHz of channels, and it cannot hop with a connection. Fine for looking at one advertising channel, useless as a real BLE sniffer - use Sniffle on TI hardware.

wifi_scan_24.note: You can see 2.4 GHz energy and demodulate with enough GNU Radio work, but 20 MHz bandwidth and 8-bit samples make this a research exercise, not a Wi-Fi tool.

packet_capture.note: Captures raw I/Q, not packets. Turning I/Q into packets is entirely on you and your host software.

scriptable.note: libhackrf C API plus Python bindings; first-class GNU Radio, SDRangel, SDR++ and gqrx support.

standalone_untethered.note: Needs a host computer over USB unless you bolt on a PortaPack.

legal.notes: Owning and receiving with a HackRF is legal in most countries, and listening across the spectrum is generally unrestricted in the US (with the notable exception of intercepting cellular voice). Transmitting is a completely different matter: HackRF can transmit on aviation, emergency services, cellular and satellite bands, and doing so without a licence is a criminal offence in nearly every jurisdiction. In the US that is FCC Part 15/301 territory and can carry very large fines. Even a low-power test transmission should go into a shielded enclosure or a dummy load, not an antenna. Check your local regulator before you key up.

ecosystem.app_store: No - it is a peripheral; software lives on the host (GNU Radio, SDRangel, SDR++, Universal Radio Hacker)

sources.what: official specs: 1 MHz-6 GHz, half-duplex, 20 Msps, 8-bit I/Q, antenna port power
official IC list: LPC43xx, CoolRunner-II CPLD, MAX2837/MAX2839, RFFC5072, MAX5864, Si5351, W25Q80BV
US reseller price $330 and statement that it is replaced by HackRF Pro
Adafruit price $339.95, 'no longer stocked'

research_gaps: Great Scott Gadgets does not publish a TX power figure in dBm; measured values in the community vary widely by frequency and I could not find an official number.
Could not confirm whether GSG intends to formally discontinue HackRF One or keep it in production alongside HackRF Pro - resellers and the vendor site disagree.

name: HackRF Pro
firmware_note: Same firmware tree and same host software as HackRF One - out of the box it behaves like a HackRF One with better analogue performance.
price_note: $400 from Hacker Warehouse. Great Scott Gadgets has publicly flagged that some units from production run r1.2.1-p1 have USB connector reliability problems - check which run you are getting.
skill_note: Identical learning curve to HackRF One; the improvements are analogue, not conceptual.
build_note: Assembled. USB-C now, so the old micro-USB cable problem goes away. Antenna still not included.
summary: The 2025 successor to HackRF One: same architecture and same software, but 100 kHz to 6 GHz instead of 1 MHz, a built-in TCXO, an FPGA in place of the CPLD, RF shielding, USB-C, and the notorious centre-frequency DC spike removed. It is the HackRF you buy new today.
honest_take: It fixes the annoyances rather than the fundamentals. It is still half-duplex and still 8-bit at full rate, so the dynamic-range and simultaneous-TX/RX limits of the original are unchanged - the extended-precision 16-bit mode only works at low sample rates. Worth the extra $70 over a HackRF One mostly for the built-in TCXO and the missing DC spike, both of which you would otherwise pay for or work around. If you already own a working HackRF One, this is not an upgrade that unlocks new attacks.
best_for: Buying a new HackRF in 2026
HF work down to 100 kHz without an external upconverter
Anyone who was going to add a TCXO to a HackRF One anyway
not_for: Full-duplex work - it is still half-duplex
High-dynamic-range receiving at full sample rate
Existing HackRF One owners looking for new capability

hardware.mcu_primary_note: Carried over from HackRF One. Increased RAM and flash versus the original.
hardware.gpio: Expansion headers retained for compatibility with existing HackRF accessories
notable_physical: Built-in TCXO
Installed RF shielding
FPGA replaces the CoolRunner-II CPLD

sdr_rx.note: 100 kHz to 6 GHz operating, tunable to 7.1 GHz. Flatter frequency response than HackRF One and no DC spike at centre frequency.

sdr_tx.note: Same range. TX power figures not published by the vendor.

sdr_bandwidth.note: Up to 20 Msps at 8-bit. A half-precision 4-bit mode reaches 40 Msps; an extended-precision 16-bit mode is available only at low sample rates.

sdr_full_duplex.note: Still half-duplex. The architectural limit was not changed.

subghz_rx.note: Part of the continuous tuning range.

subghz_tx.note: Part of the continuous tuning range.

scriptable.note: Binary-compatible with existing HackRF host software - libhackrf, GNU Radio, SDRangel, SDR++.

standalone_untethered.note: Host-tethered unless paired with a PortaPack.

legal.notes: Same position as HackRF One: receiving is broadly permitted, transmitting on licensed bands without authorisation is a criminal offence in most countries. The wider 100 kHz low end adds LF and the AM broadcast band to what you can accidentally transmit into. Check your local regulator; use a dummy load or shielded enclosure for testing.

sources.what: official specs: 100 kHz-6 GHz, tunable to 7.1 GHz, half-duplex, 20 Msps, 8-bit with 16-bit extended and 4-bit half-precision modes, TCXO, FPGA, no DC spike
vendor notice that some r1.2.1-p1 units have USB connector reliability issues
US reseller price $400

research_gaps: No published TX power specification.
Exact FPGA part number not stated in the material I could reach.

name: HackRF + PortaPack H4M
firmware_note: Mayhem is the community firmware that turns the PortaPack from a screen into an actual standalone tool - it supplies the spectrum analyser, the capture/replay apps, ADS-B, POCSAG, AIS and the rest.
vendor: OpenSourceSDRLab (PortaPack H4M design); Mayhem firmware by the portapack-mayhem community
price_note: $190 for the H4M board alone at Hacker Warehouse (HackRF NOT included; out of stock at time of checking). OpenSourceSDRLab sells a complete bundle for around $152 that includes a HackRF - but that bundled HackRF is a clone, not a Great Scott Gadgets unit. A genuine HackRF One is ~$330 on its own, which is why the clone bundles dominate the market.
skill_note: Mayhem's menus make individual functions easy to launch, but interpreting what you see - and knowing which buttons are illegal to press - still needs RF knowledge.
build_note: The PortaPack seats onto the HackRF's internal headers and screws into a shared case - no soldering, but you will need to flash Mayhem yourself unless the seller pre-flashed it.
summary: A screen, battery, speaker and navigation controls that bolt onto a HackRF to make it a standalone handheld radio tool, with the community Mayhem firmware doing the actual work. The H4M is the 2025-generation board from OpenSourceSDRLab, adding USB-C, a real power switch, a speaker and microphone, a proper battery fuel gauge, a matte 3.2-inch touchscreen and an I2C-capable GPIO port.
honest_take: Read this part carefully: Great Scott Gadgets does not make the PortaPack and never has. The original was a ShareBrained Technology design from 2014, ShareBrained stopped manufacturing years ago, and what you can buy today is a field of third-party boards of wildly varying quality. Almost every 'HackRF PortaPack' bundle on Amazon and AliExpress ships a cloned HackRF, so you are buying clone silicon and sending nothing to the people who designed it. The hardware is also not the product - Mayhem is. Without Mayhem the PortaPack is a screen that does very little, and the radio underneath is still an 8-bit half-duplex HackRF with all the same limits.
best_for: Field RF work with no laptop
Learning what signals look like, hands-on, away from a desk
Demos, conference badges-adjacent tinkering, and physical red-team recon
not_for: Anyone expecting Great Scott Gadgets quality control or support
Serious DSP - the on-board processing is far weaker than a laptop
Buying an H3: it uses proprietary firmware nobody maintains

hardware.mcu_primary_note: The PortaPack has no application processor of its own - Mayhem runs on the HackRF's own LPC43xx (the M4 and M0 cores). The PortaPack supplies display, audio, controls, battery and storage.
hardware.battery_note: Li-ion with a dedicated fuel-gauge IC reporting real percentage, voltage and current draw in firmware. A sliding switch fully disconnects the battery, fixing the H2's phantom-drain and accidental-power-on-in-a-bag problem.
hardware.gpio: I2C-capable GPIO header for user add-ons - new in H4M, not present on earlier PortaPacks
hardware.case: Varies by seller; transparent and aluminium options sold
notable_physical: Built-in speaker and microphone with automatic headphone switching
Real-time clock with backup cell
Rotary encoder plus navigation buttons
Dedicated sliding power switch

sdr_rx.note: Inherits the HackRF's 1 MHz-6 GHz (or 100 kHz on a Pro). Mayhem adds an on-screen waterfall and spectrum analyser.

sdr_tx.note: Mayhem exposes transmit apps directly on the device. This is exactly where people get themselves in legal trouble.

sdr_bandwidth.note: Adjustable 2-20 Msps, but on-device processing is far more limited than a host PC - most Mayhem apps work on narrow slices.

subghz_rx.note: Mayhem includes capture, replay and OOK/key-fob demodulation apps.

subghz_tx.note: Includes an OOK/remote transmit app and a raw replay app.

subghz_replay.note: Capture-to-SD then replay is a headline Mayhem feature and works on fixed-code remotes.

subghz_rolling_code.note: No rolling-code defeat. Replaying a captured KeeLoq/rolling transmission does not open the gate; this is the single most common misconception about the device.

subghz_bruteforce.note: Mayhem has brute-force apps for some fixed-code formats (e.g. de Bruijn sequences for simple OOK). Ineffective against anything modern.

ble_sniff.note: Mayhem has a BLE receive/advertising app, but it is a narrow-slice look at advertising channels - it cannot follow connections. Not a substitute for Sniffle or an nRF Sniffer.

ble_advertise.note: Mayhem can transmit crafted BLE advertising frames. Effectiveness varies and it is not a full BLE stack.

wifi_scan_24.note: Energy/spectrum view in the 2.4 GHz band, not an 802.11 scanner. It does not associate, decode SSIDs reliably, or capture handshakes.

gps.note: PortaPack boards have an optional GPS module header; Mayhem supports it for timestamping and some apps. Not fitted by default on most units.

sd_logging.note: Captures and logs write to microSD.

standalone_untethered.note: This is the entire point - runs on its own battery with no computer.

app_store.note: No app store. Apps are compiled into the Mayhem firmware image; you update by flashing a new release.

legal.notes: This is the highest-legal-risk item in this batch, because it puts one-button transmit into a handheld you can carry around. Listening is generally lawful; Mayhem's transmit apps can put you on aviation, marine (AIS), pager, emergency and cellular-adjacent frequencies where transmitting without a licence is a criminal offence in most countries. Replaying a captured signal to open a gate or barrier you do not own is a separate offence again in most jurisdictions, regardless of licensing. Check your local regulator and do transmit testing into a dummy load.

ecosystem.app_store: No - apps ship inside the firmware image; stable and nightly builds on GitHub

sources.what: Mayhem supports H1/H2/H4/H4M, GPL-3.0, warns against H3 clones running unmaintained proprietary firmware
independent review: H4M made by OpenSourceSDRLab, ~$152 bundle includes a HackRF clone, list of H4M improvements
ShareBrained confirms it created the original PortaPack, no longer manufactures it, and that many third-party variants now exist
US reseller price $190, HackRF explicitly not included, Mayhem must be flashed

research_gaps: The H4M is a closed commercial design; I could not find published schematics, so the display controller, audio codec and fuel-gauge part numbers are unknown.
Could not confirm whether the H4M's HackRF-side compatibility extends to HackRF Pro.

name: HackRF + PortaPack H2
firmware_note: Same Mayhem firmware as the H4M; the firmware detects which PortaPack generation it is running on.
vendor: Multiple third-party manufacturers (no single official vendor)
price_note: Estimate. There is no official vendor and no official price - H2 boards and H2+HackRF-clone bundles circulate on AliExpress, Amazon and eBay from roughly $100 to $200 depending on what clone radio is bundled and whether a case and battery are included. Quality is a genuine lottery.
skill_note: Same as the H4M, plus the extra burden of working out whether the board you received is a good one.
build_note: Plugs onto the HackRF headers. Many sellers ship with old or proprietary firmware; expect to flash Mayhem yourself.
summary: The previous-generation PortaPack and still the most widely sold. It does the same job as the H4M - screen, controls, battery, microSD, standalone operation of a HackRF via Mayhem - with an older resistive-feeling screen, micro-USB, no speaker on the base variants, and voltage-only battery monitoring.
honest_take: The H2's specific defects are worth knowing before you buy the cheaper option: the encoder knob doubles as the power control and routinely switches the unit on inside a bag, and battery monitoring is a crude voltage reading rather than a fuel gauge. The bigger risk is the counterfeit tier below it - 'H3' boards use proprietary firmware that Mayhem does not support and nobody maintains, and boards that look visually different from the reference design or arrive with a bundled firmware .bin file are a warning sign. If your budget stretches, the H4M fixes essentially all of this.
best_for: The cheapest route to a standalone Mayhem handheld
People who already own a HackRF and want to try the form factor
not_for: Anyone who wants a supported product with a warranty
Buyers who cannot tell a good clone from a bad one
Long unattended runs - the phantom battery drain is real

hardware.battery_note: Battery capacity varies by seller. Monitoring is by voltage estimate only, not a fuel-gauge IC.

legal.notes: Identical to the H4M: receiving is generally lawful, one-button transmitting on licensed bands is not, and replaying a captured signal to actuate something you do not own is usually a separate offence. Check your local regulator.

name: RTL-SDR Blog V4
firmware_note: There is no user firmware - the RTL2832U is a fixed-function USB device. The 'driver' is the host-side librtlsdr fork that knows about the V4's R828D tuner and upconverter.
price_note: The V4 has been end-of-lifed and is no longer listed in the RTL-SDR Blog store. The current model is the RTL-SDR Blog V4L (Lite) at $37.95, which uses an R828S tuner instead of the V4's R828D. The older V3 remains on sale at $34.95-$39.95 (dongle only) or $44.95-$49.95 with the dipole antenna kit. If you are buying today you are buying a V4L or a V3, not a V4.
skill_note: Plug it in, install SDR++ or SDRSharp, and you are listening in about ten minutes. There is no way to break anything or break the law with it.
build_note: USB dongle. The bundled dipole kit (on the antenna bundles) is genuinely good and covers most beginner projects.
summary: A $40 receive-only USB software-defined radio covering roughly 500 kHz to 1.766 GHz, built on the RTL2832U demodulator with an R828D tuner and a built-in upconverter for HF. It is the entry point that the whole SDR hobby is built on, and it is the correct first purchase for almost everyone.
honest_take: Buy this first. Seriously - if you are reading a comparison page trying to decide between a HackRF and something else, the honest answer is that you should spend $40 here and learn what a waterfall is before spending $330. It receives only: there is no transmit path, no DAC, no way to make it transmit, and that is a feature, not a limitation - it means you cannot accidentally commit a felony while learning. The real limits are the 8-bit ADC, the ~2.4 Msps of usable bandwidth, and the 1.766 GHz ceiling. Note also that the V4 specifically is now end-of-life; the V4L that replaced it uses a different tuner.
best_for: Absolutely anyone starting in RF or SDR
ADS-B aircraft tracking, weather satellites, pagers, trunked radio, AIS
HF/shortwave listening without a separate upconverter
A cheap second receiver alongside a HackRF
not_for: Transmitting anything, ever - there is no transmitter
Above 1.766 GHz (no 2.4 GHz, no Wi-Fi, no BLE)
Wide captures - usable bandwidth is about 2.4 MHz
Weak signals next to strong ones - it is 8-bit

hardware.mcu_primary_note: Realtek DVB-T demodulator repurposed as a raw 8-bit I/Q sampler over USB. This chip is the entire reason cheap SDR exists.

radios.note: Rafael Micro tuner with three switchable inputs, which is what allows the V4's triplexed HF/VHF/UHF input filtering. The V3 used the single-input R860 (R820T2); the replacement V4L uses an R828S.
Double-balanced mixer forming a built-in upconverter that shifts HF up by 28.8 MHz, so HF works with no external hardware and without the V3's Nyquist folding around 14.4 MHz.

hardware.gpio: None
hardware.case: Aluminium shell (acts as a heat sink and shield)
notable_physical: 1 PPM TCXO
Software-enabled bias tee with an LED indicator
Triplexed input filtering giving 28-43 dB of out-of-band isolation

sdr_rx.note: 500 kHz to 1.766 GHz. HF below ~24 MHz goes through the internal upconverter.

sdr_tx.note: Receive only. There is no DAC and no transmit path in the hardware. No firmware or software can change this.

sdr_bandwidth.note: The RTL2832U will claim 3.2 Msps but drops samples above about 2.4 Msps on most hosts. Treat ~2.4 MHz as the real usable bandwidth.

sdr_full_duplex.note: Not applicable - it cannot transmit at all.

subghz_rx.note: The 300-928 MHz remote-control and ISM bands are comfortably inside its range; rtl_433 decodes hundreds of device protocols.

gps.note: It can receive GPS L1 at 1575 MHz with an active antenna and the bias tee, but 8-bit sampling makes GNSS decoding marginal.

packet_capture.note: Captures I/Q; rtl_433, dump1090 and multimon-ng turn that into decoded packets for many protocols.

scriptable.note: librtlsdr C API, pyrtlsdr, GNU Radio, SoapySDR. Enormous tooling ecosystem.

standalone_untethered.note: Needs a host - though a Raspberry Pi is a perfectly good host.

legal.notes: About as low-risk as security hardware gets, because it physically cannot transmit. Owning and using one is legal essentially everywhere. The caveats are about what you listen to, not the device: intercepting cellular calls is specifically prohibited in the US, some European countries restrict monitoring emergency-services or non-broadcast traffic, and acting on or disclosing what you overhear can be an offence even where listening is not. Check your local law on scanner/monitoring rules.

ecosystem.app_store: No - but the host software ecosystem (SDR++, SDRSharp, gqrx, rtl_433, dump1090, SDRangel) is the largest of any SDR

sources.what: official V4 specs: R828D tuner, 500 kHz-1.766 GHz, SA612 upconverter at 28.8 MHz, 1 PPM TCXO, bias tee, triplexed filtering 28-43 dB
V4 EOL confirmation and current pricing: V4L (R828S) $37.95, V3 $34.95-$49.95
confirms the product line is receive-only

research_gaps: RTL-SDR Blog does not publish a formal datasheet stating the ADC bit depth; 8-bit is the well-established RTL2832U figure but I could not confirm it from an official V4 document in this pass.
Could not find a dedicated V4L announcement post explaining exactly why the V4 was end-of-lifed or how the R828S differs in practice from the R828D.

name: YARD Stick One
firmware_note: Ships with RfCat pre-installed - it gives you an interactive Python shell that drives the radio directly, which is the whole point of the device.
price_note: $140 at Hacker Warehouse, in stock. Case +$20, antenna +$25-30. Antenna is not included and you need one for your band.
skill_note: You drive it from a Python shell and you must already know your target's modulation, data rate, deviation and encoding - it will not find them for you.
build_note: Assembled USB stick. Bare board unless you buy the case.
summary: A sub-1 GHz half-duplex transceiver built on a TI CC1111 with RX and TX amplifiers, driven from Python via RfCat. It is not an SDR - it is a configurable protocol radio, which means it is far better than a HackRF at actually talking to a specific device once you know that device's radio parameters.
honest_take: The common mistake is comparing it to a HackRF on frequency coverage and concluding it is worse. Different tool: a HackRF gives you raw samples across 6 GHz and leaves the demodulation to you, while a YARD Stick One demodulates in hardware and hands you bytes - which is dramatically more practical for actually interacting with a garage door or a sensor. The flip side is that you must know the modulation and data rate in advance, so people usually reach for an RTL-SDR or HackRF first to characterise a signal and a YARD Stick One second to talk to it. Note the official frequency ranges have gaps; the wider 'unofficial' ranges work in practice but are not guaranteed. It is also a decade old and RfCat development is slow.
best_for: Interacting with a sub-GHz protocol once you know its parameters
Fuzzing and scripted RF work from Python
Key-fob, sensor and alarm research
The device that pairs naturally with an RTL-SDR for reconnaissance
not_for: Signal discovery - it cannot show you a waterfall
Anything above 1 GHz (no 2.4 GHz, no BLE, no Wi-Fi)
Beginners - RfCat assumes you already understand modulation parameters
Rolling-code defeat

hardware.mcu_primary_note: 8051 core with an integrated sub-GHz transceiver and USB - the MCU and the radio are the same chip, which is why it can demodulate in hardware and stream bytes.

radios.note: Official: 300-348, 391-464, 782-928 MHz. Unofficial (works in GSG's experience, not guaranteed): 281-361, 378-481, 749-962 MHz.

hardware.gpio: Test points / programming header for CC Bootloader; not a general-purpose GPIO product
hardware.case: Bare board; optional case sold separately
notable_physical: Separate RX and TX amplifiers
SMA antenna connector
CC Bootloader allows firmware updates over USB without a programmer

subghz_rx.note: 300-348, 391-464, 782-928 MHz officially; hardware-demodulated to bytes rather than raw I/Q.

subghz_tx.note: Same ranges. Half-duplex - it cannot listen while transmitting.

subghz_replay.note: Straightforward in RfCat once you have set the correct modulation and data rate.

subghz_rolling_code.note: No rolling-code capability. It is a radio, not a cryptanalysis tool.

subghz_bruteforce.note: Scriptable from Python, which makes it a natural brute-force platform for fixed-code systems - and useless against modern ones.

subghz_amplified.note: Both RX and TX amplifiers are on board. GSG does not publish an output figure in dBm.

sdr_rx.note: Not an SDR. It is a fixed-architecture transceiver - you get demodulated bytes, never raw I/Q, and there is no waterfall.

scriptable.note: RfCat gives an interactive Python shell (rfcat -r) plus an importable library. This is its defining feature.

standalone_untethered.note: Needs a host over USB.

legal.notes: Receiving on sub-GHz is generally lawful. Transmitting is where the risk is: the device's ranges cover licensed land-mobile, amateur, paging and public-safety allocations as well as licence-exempt ISM bands, and transmitting outside the ISM allocations without a licence is an offence in most countries. Separately, transmitting to actuate a gate, garage, alarm or vehicle you do not own is typically a criminal offence in its own right regardless of frequency. Check your local regulator's ISM band plan before transmitting.

ecosystem.app_store: No - RfCat is a Python library and shell

sources.what: official specs: frequency ranges official and unofficial, ASK/OOK/GFSK/2-FSK/4-FSK/MSK, up to 500 kbps, half-duplex, RfCat preinstalled
RfCat firmware and Python host library
US price $140, in stock, confirms RX and TX amplifiers and SMA connector

summary: A full-duplex 12-bit SDR covering 10 MHz to 3.5 GHz with 40 MHz of bandwidth, built on the LMS7002M transceiver and a Lattice ECP5 FPGA with 44K LUTs of user-accessible logic. honest_take: This is a development platform that happens to be usable for security work, not a security tool. Its two genuine advantages over a HackRF are that it is full duplex and 12-bit, which matter enormously if you are implementing a protocol that must respond to what it hears - a HackRF simply cannot do that. Against it: narrower coverage (3.5 GHz vs 6 GHz), a much smaller community, a rougher software story around LimeSuite, and a price that buys a HackRF Pro with change. summary: A $20 Zigbee dongle whose TI CC2652P is exactly the silicon NCC Group's Sniffle targets. honest_take: This is the answer to 'what should I actually buy to sniff BLE', and almost nobody knows it. Watching all three advertising channels at once is not a nice-to-have - it is the difference between catching the connection request and missing it, and Sniffle's own documentation puts connection detection at roughly three times more reliable than single-channel sniffers. It beats a retired $125 Ubertooth and a $11 Nordic dongle on capability while sitting between them on price. The catches are real but small: you must flash it yourself, doing so removes the Zigbee function, and Sniffle is a link-layer capture tool - it does not break encryption, and a connection using LE Secure Connections pairing will be captured but not readable.

honest_take: It is a bench tool for talking to chips, not an attack tool. The genuinely useful part is not the protocol support - a $5 FTDI cable does UART - it is the current-limited programmable supply and the live per-pin voltage display, which between them stop you from destroying the target while you work out what its pinout is. honest_take: This is the boring, correct answer for most hardware hacking, and the honest pitch is that it saves you from a drawer full of cheap FTDI breakouts that all run at 3.3 V and quietly damage 1.8 V targets. Its limits are real though: FT2232H means two channels, so you get one dedicated UART plus one shared port that must be switched between SPI/JTAG and I2C/SWD, and its 'logic analyzer port' is a header for your own analyser, not a built-in one. name: Cynthion
firmware_note: The FPGA gateware is LUNA, the debug controller firmware is Apollo, and the capture UI is Packetry - all open source and all separately replaceable.
price_note: $209.95 at Adafruit for the version with the milled aluminium enclosure, out of stock at time of checking. A bare-board version sells for roughly $150. Note the name: this shipped as 'Cynthion' in September 2024 after being developed under the name LUNA.
skill_note: Packetry makes capture straightforward, but reading USB descriptors, transfers and endpoint traffic is a skill in itself.
build_note: Assembled, optionally in a milled aluminium case. Critically, no USB cables are included and you will need several A and C cables to wire host, target and control.
summary: An FPGA-based USB test instrument that captures Low, Full and High Speed USB 2.0 traffic between a host and a device, and can also emulate devices itself. It pairs Packetry for analysis with Facedancer for emulation, at a fraction of the price of commercial USB protocol analysers.
honest_take: The value proposition is straightforward and real: commercial High-Speed USB protocol analysers start in the low thousands, and this does the core job for around $200 with open gateware you can modify. The limit to be clear about is that it is USB 2.0 only - Low, Full and High Speed. It does not capture SuperSpeed (USB 3.x), so a USB 3 device negotiating SuperSpeed will fall back or be invisible; Great Scott Gadgets has a separate 'LUNA SuperSpeed' project in development for that. Also budget for cables, because none are in the box and you need three connections to use it properly.

name: Facedancer
firmware_note: Facedancer is Python software, not a board. It drives a remote-controlled USB controller on hardware you already own.
price_note: The software is free and BSD-3-Clause licensed. You need supported hardware to run it: a Cynthion (~$150-210) or a GreatFET One ($90) are the current mainstream options. The original dedicated 'Facedancer21' boards are legacy.
skill_note: You write Python that implements a USB device class by hand - descriptors, endpoints, control transfers. It assumes you understand the USB specification.
build_note: pip install the library and point it at supported hardware. No soldering, but real programming.
summary: A Python framework for emulating USB devices in software, using a piece of supported hardware as the remote-controlled USB controller. It is the standard tool for USB host fuzzing, protocol man-in-the-middle, and building a fake USB device to see how a host reacts.
honest_take: The confusion worth clearing up is that 'Facedancer' names three things: the original dedicated boards from Travis Goodspeed's GoodFET lineage, the modern Python library, and loosely the whole technique. What you install today is the library, and the hardware you run it on is almost always a Cynthion or a GreatFET One. It is genuinely powerful - being able to write a USB device in Python and watch a host's driver fall over is a rare capability - but it is a framework, not a tool. There is no menu, no payload library and no GUI. If you want a USB attack device that just works, this is not it; if you want to write one, this is what you build it on.
